notes.definition: Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points because a lot of energy is needed to break the many strong ionic bonds, and they conduct electricity only when melted or dissolved in water, when their ions are free to move.
explanation: Ionic compounds have regular structures called giant ionic lattices. In these lattices there are strong electrostatic forces of attraction acting in all directions between oppositely charged ions. Every ion is held by attractions to all the ions of opposite charge around it, and there are a huge number of these attractions throughout the giant structure.

Ionic compounds have high melting points and high boiling points. This is because large amounts of energy are needed to break the many strong bonds. To melt an ionic solid, enough energy must be transferred to overcome many of the electrostatic forces so that the ions can move past each other. For example, sodium chloride melts at 801 °C and boils at 1413 °C, so all ionic compounds are solids at room temperature. When answering exam questions, mention all three ideas: the bonds are strong, there are many of them, and a lot of energy is needed to overcome them.

When melted or dissolved in water, ionic compounds conduct electricity because the ions are free to move and so charge can flow. In a solid ionic compound the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice. They can vibrate but cannot move from place to place, so the solid does not conduct electricity. When the compound is melted (molten) or dissolved to form an aqueous solution, the lattice breaks up and the ions can move. Positive ions move towards the negative electrode and negative ions towards the positive electrode, carrying charge through the liquid. This is the basis of electrolysis.

Remember that it is the ions that move in a molten or dissolved ionic compound, not electrons. Ionic compounds do not have delocalised electrons. The strength of the forces can also differ between ionic compounds: ions with larger charges, such as Mg²⁺ and O²⁻, attract each other more strongly than ions with single charges, such as Na⁺ and Cl⁻. This is why magnesium oxide (melting point 2852 °C) has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride. You only need to know the structure of sodium chloride, but you should be able to apply these ideas to data about other ionic compounds.
keyFacts: Ionic compounds have giant ionic lattices with strong electrostatic forces in all directions between oppositely charged ions.
Ionic compounds have high melting points and high boiling points.
Large amounts of energy are needed to break the many strong bonds.
Ionic compounds are solids at room temperature.
Solid ionic compounds do not conduct electricity: the ions are in fixed positions.
Molten or dissolved ionic compounds conduct: the ions are free to move and carry charge.
In ionic compounds it is ions, not electrons, that move to carry the current.
Higher charges on ions (2+ and 2−) give stronger attraction and higher melting points.

keyTerms.definition: A regular three-dimensional arrangement of a very large number of oppositely charged ions.
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid.
The ability of a substance to allow an electric current (a flow of charge) to pass through it.
Melted; in the liquid state because of heating.
A solution formed when a substance dissolves in water.
A molten or dissolved ionic compound that conducts electricity because its ions are free to move.

workedExamples.title: Explaining a high melting point
workedExamples.question: Explain why potassium chloride has a high melting point (770 °C).
steps: Potassium chloride is ionic and has a giant ionic lattice.
There are strong electrostatic forces of attraction between the oppositely charged K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
There are many of these strong bonds throughout the giant structure.
A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these many strong forces.
workedExamples.answer: Giant lattice with many strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions; a large amount of energy is needed to overcome them.

workedExamples.title: Explaining conductivity
workedExamples.question: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but sodium chloride solution does. Explain why.
steps: In the solid, the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move.
When the solid dissolves, the ions separate and are free to move through the solution.
Moving ions carry charge, so the solution conducts electricity.
workedExamples.answer: Ions cannot move in the solid, but in solution the ions are free to move and carry charge.

workedExamples.title: Using data to compare ionic compounds
workedExamples.question: Sodium chloride melts at 801 °C and magnesium oxide melts at 2852 °C. Calculate the difference and suggest a reason for it.
steps: Magnesium oxide contains Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions; sodium chloride contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
Ions with higher charges attract each other more strongly.
More energy is needed to overcome the stronger forces in magnesium oxide.
workedExamples.answer: 2051 °C higher; the 2+ and 2− ions in MgO attract more strongly than 1+ and 1− ions in NaCl.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say ionic compounds conduct when molten because electrons move.
misconceptions.right: Ionic compounds have no delocalised electrons. They conduct because the ions are free to move and carry charge.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say solid ionic compounds conduct electricity because they contain charged particles.
misconceptions.right: The ions in a solid are held in fixed positions, so they cannot move and carry charge. The solid does not conduct.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write that ionic compounds have high melting points because of strong intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.right: There are no molecules in ionic compounds. The high melting point is due to strong electrostatic forces between ions (ionic bonds).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think melting an ionic compound breaks it into atoms or molecules.
misconceptions.right: Melting overcomes some of the forces between ions so they can move; the particles are still ions.

realWorld: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (dissolved in molten cryolite) because the ions must be free to move.
Magnesium oxide is used to line furnaces because its very high melting point means it does not melt at furnace temperatures.
Sweat contains dissolved ions, which is why electrical equipment should not be handled with wet hands: the solution conducts.
examTips: For melting point questions use all three ideas: 'giant lattice', 'many strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions', 'a lot of energy needed to overcome them'.
For conductivity questions say 'ions are free to move and carry charge' when molten or dissolved. Never say electrons move in an ionic compound.
Say why the solid does not conduct: 'ions are in fixed positions and cannot move'.
Never use 'intermolecular forces' or 'molecules' when writing about ionic compounds.
summary: Ionic compounds form giant lattices with strong electrostatic forces in all directions.
They have high melting and boiling points: lots of energy is needed to break many strong bonds.
They do not conduct when solid because the ions cannot move.
They conduct when melted or dissolved because the ions are free to move and carry charge.
Higher ion charges mean stronger attraction and higher melting points.

questions.question: Why does sodium chloride have a high melting point?
options: A lot of energy is needed to break the many strong ionic bonds.
markScheme: 1 mark: A lot of energy is needed to break the many strong ionic bonds.
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride is ionic: many strong electrostatic forces must be overcome. It has no molecules, intermolecular forces or covalent bonds.

questions.question: Under which conditions does sodium chloride conduct electricity?
options: When molten or dissolved in water
markScheme: 1 mark: When molten or dissolved in water
questions.explanation: The ions must be free to move, which happens when molten or dissolved, not in the solid.

questions.question: What is the state of potassium bromide at room temperature?
markScheme: 1 mark: Solid
questions.explanation: Ionic compounds have high melting points, so they are solids at room temperature.

questions.question: Why does solid sodium chloride NOT conduct electricity?
options: The ions are held in fixed positions.
markScheme: 1 mark: The ions are held in fixed positions.
questions.explanation: Solid NaCl does contain ions, but they cannot move from place to place, so no charge flows.

questions.question: Which particles carry the charge through molten lead bromide?
markScheme: 1 mark: Ions
questions.explanation: Molten ionic compounds conduct because their ions move. There are no delocalised electrons in an ionic compound.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows some properties of substance X.
What type of substance is X most likely to be?
markScheme: 1 mark: An ionic compound
questions.explanation: High melting point plus conducting only when molten is typical of an ionic compound. Metals conduct when solid; small molecules have low melting points and do not conduct.

questions.question: Which phrase best describes the forces holding an ionic lattice together?
options: Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions in all directions
Shared pairs of electrons between atoms
Forces between positive ions and delocalised electrons
markScheme: 1 mark: Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions in all directions
questions.explanation: Ionic lattices are held by strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, acting in all directions.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting points of calcium oxide and potassium chloride.
Which is the best explanation for the difference in melting points?
options: Calcium oxide has stronger covalent bonds.
Ca²⁺ and O²⁻ have larger charges than K⁺ and Cl⁻, so the electrostatic attraction is stronger.
Potassium chloride has weak intermolecular forces.
markScheme: 1 mark: Ca²⁺ and O²⁻ have larger charges than K⁺ and Cl⁻, so the electrostatic attraction is stronger.
questions.explanation: Both are ionic. Ions with 2+ and 2− charges attract each other more strongly, so more energy is needed to melt calcium oxide.

questions.question:
A student says: 'Molten sodium chloride conducts because electrons flow through it, like in a metal.'
Why is the student wrong?
options: Molten sodium chloride does not conduct.
The current is carried by moving ions, not electrons.
Only protons can flow in a liquid.
Electrons flow only in solid sodium chloride.
markScheme: 1 mark: The current is carried by moving ions, not electrons.
questions.explanation: Ionic compounds have no delocalised electrons. In the molten state the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions move to the electrodes, carrying charge.

questions.question:
A solid ionic compound is heated and its electrical conductivity is measured.
At what point does the compound start to conduct electricity?
options: As soon as it is warmed
At its melting point, when the ions become free to move
At its boiling point, when it becomes a gas
markScheme: 1 mark: At its melting point, when the ions become free to move
questions.explanation: The ions become free to move when the lattice breaks down on melting, so the compound starts to conduct at its melting point.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting point and boiling point of sodium chloride.
Calculate the temperature range over which sodium chloride is a liquid.
questions.explanation: Range = boiling point − melting point = 1413 − 801 = 612 °C.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting points of two ionic compounds.
Calculate how much higher the melting point of magnesium oxide is than the melting point of sodium chloride.

Table 1 shows the melting points of four ionic compounds.
Calculate the mean melting point of the four compounds.

Potassium chloride melts at 770 °C.
A sample of solid potassium chloride at 20 °C is heated. The temperature rises at a steady rate of 50 °C per minute.
Calculate the time before the sample starts to conduct electricity.
markScheme: 1 mark: temperature rise needed = 770 − 20 = 750 °C
1 mark: 750 ÷ 50 = 15 minutes
questions.explanation: It conducts once it melts (ions free to move). 770 − 20 = 750 °C rise; at 50 °C per minute this takes 750 ÷ 50 = 15 minutes.

questions.question: Give two properties of ionic compounds.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: high melting point; high boiling point; conduct electricity when molten or dissolved; do not conduct when solid; solid at room temperature
questions.explanation: These properties all come from the giant lattice of strongly attracted ions.

questions.question: State what must be able to move for a substance to conduct electricity.
markScheme: 1 mark: charged particles (ions or electrons)
questions.explanation: Electric current is a flow of charge, which needs mobile charged particles.

questions.question: Explain why magnesium chloride has a high melting point.
markScheme: 1 mark: giant (ionic) lattice / structure
1 mark: strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions
1 mark: (many bonds so) large amount of energy needed to overcome them
questions.explanation: Three separate ideas earn the three marks: structure, strong forces and energy.

questions.question: Explain why sodium chloride solution conducts electricity.
markScheme: 1 mark: the ions are free to move (when dissolved)
1 mark: so they can carry charge / charge can flow
questions.explanation: In solution the lattice has broken up and the ions move through the water.

questions.question:
A student tests a white solid.
Table 1 shows the student's results.
Suggest one further test the student could do to show that the solid is ionic.
Give the expected result.
markScheme: 1 mark: dissolve it in water (or melt it) and test whether it conducts
1 mark: it would conduct electricity
questions.explanation: Conducting only when molten or dissolved, together with a high melting point, is good evidence of ionic bonding.

questions.question: Explain why an ionic compound conducts electricity when molten but not when it is a solid. Refer to the movement of particles.
markScheme: 1 mark: in the solid the ions are in fixed positions / can only vibrate
1 mark: when molten the ions are free to move and carry charge
questions.explanation: Both states contain ions; the difference is whether the ions can move.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting points of sodium fluoride and sodium chloride.
Both compounds contain 1+ and 1− ions.
Suggest why sodium fluoride has the higher melting point.
markScheme: 1 mark: fluoride ions are smaller than chloride ions, so the ions are closer together
1 mark: stronger electrostatic attraction, so more energy is needed to overcome it
questions.explanation: The charges are the same, so the difference must come from ion size: smaller ions can get closer, increasing the attraction.

questions.question: Which set of properties shows that a substance is ionic?
options: Low melting point; does not conduct in any state
High melting point; conducts when solid and when molten
Low melting point; conducts when dissolved only
High melting point; conducts when molten but not when solid
markScheme: 1 mark: High melting point; conducts when molten but not when solid
questions.explanation: Ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct only when the ions are free to move (molten or dissolved). Conducting when solid suggests a metal.

questions.question: Explain why all ionic compounds are solids at room temperature.
markScheme: 1 mark: strong electrostatic forces between (oppositely charged) ions
1 mark: so they have high melting points, well above room temperature / a lot of energy is needed to melt them
questions.explanation: Room temperature (about 20 °C) does not supply nearly enough energy to overcome the many strong ionic bonds.

questions.question: To extract sodium by electrolysis, sodium chloride must be molten rather than solid. Explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: in the solid the ions cannot move / are in fixed positions
1 mark: when molten the ions are free to move to the electrodes (and carry charge)
questions.explanation: Electrolysis needs the ions to move to the electrodes, which only happens once the lattice has broken down.

questions.question: Explain the electrical conductivity of sodium chloride in the solid, molten and dissolved states.
markScheme: Indicative content: solid: ions present but held in fixed positions in the lattice; cannot move; does not conduct. Molten: lattice broken down; ions free to move; carry charge; conducts. Dissolved: ions separate and are free to move in the solution; carry charge; conducts. No delocalised electrons in an ionic compound; current is carried by ions.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): all three states correctly explained in terms of whether the ions can move and carry charge
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): correct statements about which states conduct, with limited explanation
questions.explanation: The deciding factor is mobility of ions: fixed in the solid, free to move when molten or dissolved.

questions.question:
A student is given three unlabelled solids, P, Q and R.
One is an ionic compound, one is a metal and one is a substance made of small molecules.
Table 1 shows the student's results.
Identify the ionic compound and explain its properties in terms of structure and bonding.
Explain why the other two solids are not ionic.
markScheme: Indicative content: R is ionic; high melting point because giant ionic lattice; many strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions in all directions; large amount of energy to overcome; does not conduct as a solid because ions in fixed positions; conducts when molten or dissolved because ions free to move and carry charge. P is not ionic: low melting point and never conducts, so small molecules with weak intermolecular forces and no charged particles. Q is not ionic: conducts as a solid, which ionic compounds cannot do; consistent with a metal with delocalised electrons.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): R correctly identified with a full explanation of both melting point and conductivity, and clear reasons for rejecting P and Q
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): R correctly identified with an explanation of at least one property, and some reasoning about P or Q
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): R identified with little or no explanation, or some correct statements about properties
questions.explanation: Conducting only when molten or dissolved is the decisive test for an ionic compound. A substance that conducts as a solid is a metal (or graphite); one with a low melting point that never conducts is molecular.
